Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: Discovering Language-neutral Sub-networks in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual pre-trained language models learn language-neutral representations, and what is the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models contain language-neutral sub-networks that are topologically similar across languages and can be effectively transferred for cross-lingual tasks, but this transferability decreases at higher sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that multilingual language models include separate language-neutral and language-specific components, with the language-neutral components playing a more prominent role in cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Winning tickets (sub-networks) can be found for each language and task at multiple sparsity levels, though performance degrades at higher sparsity.
Sub-networks for different languages have high parameter overlap, especially for NER and XNLI tasks, indicating language-neutral components.
Cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets is effective for XNLI and NER, but less so for MLM, and transfer performance degrades at higher sparsity.
The language-neutral components are more prominent in the middle to upper layers of the model.
Combining multiple languages during pruning can yield sub-networks that transfer better to low-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Parameter overlap may not be a fine-grained measure for identifying language-neutral components, as small differences in cross-lingual performance do not strongly correlate with overlap.
Only the lottery ticket hypothesis is used for discovering sub-networks, while other pruning and masking methods may provide complementary or competing insights.
Due to computational limitations, the analysis is limited to three tasks and eleven languages, and new insights may emerge from a larger cross-section.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models transfer remarkably well on cross-lingual downstream tasks. However, the extent to which they learn language-neutral representations (i.e., shared representations that encode similar phenomena across languages), and the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance, remain open questions. In this work, we conceptualize language neutrality of multilingual models as a function of the overlap between language-encoding subnetworks of these models. We employ the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover sub-networks that are individually optimized for various languages and tasks. Our evaluation across three distinct tasks and eleven typologically-diverse languages demonstrates that sub-networks for different languages are topologically similar (i.e., language-neutral), making them effective initializations for cross-lingual transfer with limited performance degradation. 1

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: How do Large Language Models Handle Multilingualism?
papers.research_question: How do large language models handle multilingualism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes and verifies a three-stage multilingual workflow (MWork) in LLMs, introducing PLND to detect language-specific neurons and showing how fine-tuning these neurons enhances multilingual abilities.
papers.conclusion: The verified MWork explains how LLMs handle multilingual tasks and provides an effective method for language-specific enhancement through fine-tuning language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs convert multilingual inputs to English in intermediate layers for task-solving and then revert to the original language for generation.
Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection (PLND) can identify language-specific neurons without any labeled data.
Deactivating language-specific neurons causes significant performance drops in multilingual tasks but minimal impact on English.
Fine-tuning language-specific neurons with small datasets (e.g., 400 documents) improves multilingual performance without compromising other languages.
The multilingual workflow involves understanding layers, task-solving layers for reasoning and knowledge extraction, and generation layers.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning with too many documents can lead to overfitting and performance deterioration due to disruption of original knowledge distribution.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse languages. This study explores how LLMs handle multilingualism. Based on observed language ratio shifts among layers and the relationships between network structures and certain capabilities, we hypothesize the LLM's multilingual workflow ($\texttt{MWork}$): LLMs initially understand the query, converting multilingual inputs into English for task-solving. In the intermediate layers, they employ English for thinking and incorporate multilingual knowledge with self-attention and feed-forward structures, respectively. In the final layers, LLMs generate responses aligned with the original language of the query. To verify $\texttt{MWork}$, we introduce Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection ($\texttt{PLND}$) to identify activated neurons for inputs in different languages without any labeled data. Using $\texttt{PLND}$, we validate $\texttt{MWork}$ through extensive experiments involving the deactivation of language-specific neurons across various layers and structures. Moreover, $\texttt{MWork}$ allows fine-tuning of language-specific neurons with a small dataset, enhancing multilingual abilities in a specific language without compromising others. This approach results in an average improvement of $3.6\%$ for high-resource languages and $2.3\%$ for low-resource languages across all tasks with just $400$ documents.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Language-Specific Neurons: The Key to Multilingual Capabilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models process multilingual texts, and what are the language-specific mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language activation probability entropy (LAPE) to identify language-specific neurons in LLMs, revealing that a small subset of neurons in top and bottom layers are crucial for multilingual processing and can be manipulated to steer output language.
papers.conclusion: The study provides evidence that language-specific neurons are key to multilingual capabilities in LLMs, and the LAPE method offers a way to identify and manipulate these neurons for better understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating language-specific neurons significantly impairs the model's proficiency in that language, as shown by increased perplexity and reduced generation quality.
Language-specific neurons are predominantly located in the bottom and top layers of LLMs, with bottom layers mapping inputs to a shared semantic space and top layers handling vocabulary mapping.
It is possible to steer the output language of LLMs by selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons, mitigating off-target language issues.
Low-resource languages are centered around high-resource languages in the representation space, indicating dominance relations.
Neurons in larger models tend to be more specialized for single languages rather than shared among multiple languages.
papers.limitation:
The LAPE method is relative to the presence of multiple languages and cannot establish an absolute threshold for single-language scenarios.
Criteria for distinguishing between high-resource and low-resource languages within the model need further investigation.
Managing a large number of languages and differences between various languages requires future research.
future_direction: Enhance knowledge transfer between major and minor languages.
Devise efficient strategies for continual pre-training to accommodate specific languages.
Investigate the differences between various languages in the model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable multilingual capabilities without being pre-trained on specially curated multilingual parallel corpora. It remains a challenging problem to explain the underlying mechanisms by which LLMs process multilingual texts. In this paper, we delve into the composition of Transformer architectures in LLMs to pinpoint language-specific regions. Specially, we propose a novel detection method, language activation probability entropy (LAPE), to identify language-specific neurons within LLMs. Based on LAPE, we conduct comprehensive experiments on several representative LLMs, such as LLaMA-2, BLOOM, and Mistral. Our findings indicate that LLMs' proficiency in processing a particular language is predominantly due to a small subset of neurons, primarily situated in the models' top and bottom layers. Furthermore, we showcase the feasibility to "steer" the output language of LLMs by selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons. Our research provides important evidence to the understanding and exploration of the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Revisiting Modality Invariance in a Multilingual Speech-Text Model via Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How and when do multilingual speech–text models reuse shared circuitry across modalities, and how does this reuse differ between input-language representation and output-language generation during decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-step-aware framework for cross-modal evaluation of multilingual speech-text models, revealing that cross-modal language alignment is time- and function-dependent, with representation alignment strongest at early steps and control alignment strengthening later.
papers.conclusion: Cross-modal processing in multilingual speech-text models is both time-dependent and function-dependent, highlighting the importance of generation-aware diagnostics for evaluating multilingual behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal language alignment for language-representation neurons is strongest at the first decoding step but weakens as generation proceeds, indicating a shift from shared to modality-specific processing.
Language-control neurons identified from speech transfer causally to text generation, revealing partially shared circuitry for output-language control.
The cross-modal effect ratio for language control increases at later decoding steps, showing stronger transfer of control mechanisms.
The distribution of language-selective neurons shifts from self-attention to cross-attention as decoding proceeds, indicating a transition from encoder-driven to autoregressive processing.
Cross-modal neuron overlap shows a strong diagonal (same-language) preference at the first step, which weakens at later steps.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model architecture (SeamlessM4T v2).
Reliance on AP-based neuron identification, which captures statistical associations but does not establish causal necessity.
Use of synthetic speech to control for acoustic variability, which may not fully reflect natural speech.
Asymmetries across tasks (e.g., ASR vs. text repetition) and language tags might introduce noise in neuron identification and cross-modal comparisons.
future_direction: Verify whether similar patterns hold for natural speech.
Explore more symmetric settings, such as En→X translation across modalities.
papers.abstract: Multilingual speech-text foundation models aim to process language uniformly across both modality and language, yet it remains unclear whether they internally represent the same language consistently when it is spoken versus written. We investigate this question in SeamlessM4T v2 through three complementary analyses that probe where language and modality information is encoded, how selective neurons causally influence decoding, and how concentrated this influence is across the network. We identify language- and modality-selective neurons using average-precision ranking, investigate their functional role via median-replacement interventions at inference time, and analyze activation-magnitude inequality across languages and modalities. Across experiments, we find evidence of incomplete modality invariance. Although encoder representations become increasingly language-agnostic, this compression makes it more difficult for the shared decoder to recover the language of origin when constructing modality-agnostic representations, particularly when adapting from speech to text. We further observe sharply localized modality-selective structure in cross-attention key and value projections. Finally, speech-conditioned decoding and non-dominant scripts exhibit higher activation concentration, indicating heavier reliance on a small subset of neurons, which may underlie increased brittleness across modalities and languages.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: On the Multilingual Ability of Decoder-based Pre-trained Language Models: Finding and Controlling Language-Specific Neurons
papers.research_question: How do decoder-based pre-trained language models handle multilingualism? Specifically, do language-specific neurons exist and how can they be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the existence of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs and shows that intervening on these neurons can control the language of generated text.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the activity of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs, showing their existence and controllability, which can facilitate deeper understanding and future research.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons are unique to each language with little overlap (<5%).
These neurons are mainly distributed in the first and last few layers of the model.
Intervening on a small set of language-specific neurons (top and bottom 1000) can drastically change the probability of generating text in the target language.
The distribution pattern of language-specific neurons is consistent across languages and model variants.
For conditional text generation (machine translation), intervention on language-specific neurons can improve translation accuracy and BLEU score for some models (like Llama2).
papers.limitation:
Only analyzes open models with publicly available parameters, not closed models like ChatGPT or GPT-4.
Focuses on only six languages; other languages need to be examined in future studies.
Does not analyze encoder-decoder-based PLMs (e.g., mT5) due to architectural differences.
future_direction: Proposing language-specific model-compression methods.
Proposing new fine-tuning methods for downstream tasks to facilitate generalization to languages not included in the training dataset (e.g., only fine-tuning the middle-layer parameters).
Analysis of encoder-decoder-based PLMs remains important for future work.
papers.abstract: Current decoder-based pre-trained language models (PLMs) successfully demonstrate multilingual capabilities. However, it is unclear how these models handle multilingualism. We analyze the neuron-level internal behavior of multilingual decoder-based PLMs, Specifically examining the existence of neurons that fire ``uniquely for each language'' within decoder-only multilingual PLMs. We analyze six languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Chinese, and Japanese, and show that language-specific neurons are unique, with a slight overlap (< 5%) between languages. These neurons are mainly distributed in the models' first and last few layers. This trend remains consistent across languages and models. Additionally, we tamper with less than 1% of the total neurons in each model during inference and demonstrate that tampering with a few language-specific neurons drastically changes the probability of target language occurrence in text generation.

papers.title: How Do Vision Transformers Work?
papers.research_question: How do multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) work? Specifically, what properties of MSAs improve optimization, how do MSAs differ from convolutional layers (Convs), and how can we harmonize MSAs with Convs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that MSAs in Vision Transformers act as generalized spatial smoothing, flattening loss landscapes and improving generalization, and are complementary to convolutional layers as low-pass vs. high-pass filters. Based on these insights, the paper proposes AlterNet, a model that alternates Conv and MSA blocks, which outperforms CNNs even on small datasets.
papers.conclusion: MSAs are generalized spatial smoothings that complement Convs, and harmonizing them via an alternating pattern leads to models that outperform CNNs across data regimes.
papers.key_findings:
MSAs improve accuracy and generalization by flattening loss landscapes, primarily due to data specificity rather than long-range dependency.
MSAs are low-pass filters that reduce high-frequency signals and aggregate feature maps, while Convs are high-pass filters that amplify high-frequency signals and diversify feature maps.
ViTs suffer from non-convex losses in small data regimes, which can be alleviated by large datasets or loss landscape smoothing methods.
Multi-stage neural networks behave like series connections of small individual models, and MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction.
The proposed AlterNet, which alternates Conv and MSA blocks, outperforms CNNs not only on large datasets but also on small datasets.
papers.limitation: The effects of data augmentation on loss landscapes and uncertainty calibration require further investigation.
future_direction: Further investigation into the effects of data augmentation on uncertainty calibration and loss landscapes.
papers.abstract: The success of multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) for computer vision is now indisputable. However, little is known about how MSAs work. We present fundamental explanations to help better understand the nature of MSAs. In particular, we demonstrate the following properties of MSAs and Vision Transformers (ViTs): (1) MSAs improve not only accuracy but also generalization by flattening the loss landscapes. Such improvement is primarily attributable to their data specificity, not long-range dependency. On the other hand, ViTs suffer from non-convex losses. Large datasets and loss landscape smoothing methods alleviate this problem; (2) MSAs and Convs exhibit opposite behaviors. For example, MSAs are low-pass filters, but Convs are high-pass filters. Therefore, MSAs and Convs are complementary; (3) Multi-stage neural networks behave like a series connection of small individual models. In addition, MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction. Based on these insights, we propose AlterNet, a model in which Conv blocks at the end of a stage are replaced with MSA blocks. AlterNet outperforms CNNs not only in large data regimes but also in small data regimes. The code is available at https://github.com/xxxnell/how-do-vits-work.

papers.title: Language Models as Artificial Learners: Investigating Crosslinguistic Influence
papers.research_question: How do L1 dominance and L2 proficiency affect crosslinguistic influence in language models, and can LMs serve as a computational framework to study human CLI?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language models can simulate crosslinguistic influence, showing that L1 dominance and L2 proficiency predict CLI, and provides mechanistic evidence of L1 co-activation during L2 processing.
papers.conclusion: LMs can serve as artificial learners to study CLI, and the findings suggest a hybrid account where shared structures are bidirectionally primed, while non-overlapping structures are separate-but-connected and influenced by dominance.
papers.key_findings:
CLI effects are modulated by syntactic distance: similar L1 languages cause less interference or more facilitation.
Crosslinguistic priming is bidirectional for grammatical structures but sensitive to language dominance for ungrammatical structures.
LMs show preference for non-native constructions from the same L1, especially after priming.
LogitLens shows L1 token presence during L2 processing increases with L1 dominance.
L2 neuron overlap between L1 languages correlates negatively with syntactic distance.
papers.abstract: Despite the centrality of crosslinguistic influence (CLI) to bilingualism research, human studies often yield conflicting results due to inherent experimental variance. We address these inconsistencies by using language models (LMs) as controlled statistical learners to systematically simulate CLI and isolate its underlying drivers. Specifically, we study the effect of varying the L1 language dominance and the L2 language proficiency, which we manipulate by controlling the L2 age of exposure -- defined as the training step at which the L2 is introduced. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of pretraining on L1 languages with varying syntactic distance from the L2. Using cross-linguistic priming, we analyze how activating L1 structures impacts L2 processing. Our results align with evidence from psycholinguistic studies, confirming that language dominance and proficiency are strong predictors of CLI. We further find that while priming of grammatical structures is bidirectional, the priming of ungrammatical structures is sensitive to language dominance. Finally, we provide mechanistic evidence of CLI in LMs, demonstrating that the L1 is co-activated during L2 processing and directly influences the neural circuitry recruited for the L2. More broadly, our work demonstrates that LMs can serve as a computational framework to inform theories of human CLI.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Rediscovering the Slavic Continuum in Representations Emerging from Neural Models of Spoken Language Identification
papers.research_question: Whether the emergent representations from a neural spoken language identification model reflect objective measures of language relatedness and/or non-linguists’ perception of language similarity, specifically for Slavic languages.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a robust convolutional neural network for Slavic language identification using adversarial training, and analyzes its emergent representations to show they capture language relatedness, with perceptual confusability being the best predictor of representation similarity.
papers.conclusion: The distances in the emergent language representations reflect language variation across phylogenetic and geographic dimensions, and perceptual confusability is a better predictor of representation similarities than phylogenetic and geographic distances.
papers.key_findings:
The language representation space captures language relatedness to a great extent.
Perceptual confusability between languages is the best predictor of language representation similarity.
The robust LID model significantly improves generalization across datasets with different recording conditions.
The distances in the representation space reflect geographic distances between languages.
The model's representations can reconstruct the Slavic genetic tree.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have been employed for various spoken language recognition tasks, including tasks that are multilingual by definition such as spoken language identification. In this paper, we present a neural model for Slavic language identification in speech signals and analyze its emergent representations to investigate whether they reflect objective measures of language relatedness and/or non-linguists' perception of language similarity. While our analysis shows that the language representation space indeed captures language relatedness to a great extent, we find perceptual confusability between languages in our study to be the best predictor of the language representation similarity.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: What do tokens know about their characters and how do they know it?
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained language models with subword tokenization encode character-level information, and through what mechanisms is this information acquired during training?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained language models with subword tokenization robustly encode character-level information in their token embeddings, and this knowledge is acquired through multiple mechanisms including systematic relationships between characters and syntactic features, as well as variability in tokenization.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models with subword tokenization implicitly learn substantial character-level information, and this knowledge arises from a combination of systematic form-function correlations in language and the inherent variability of subword tokenization.
papers.key_findings:
Subword-tokenized PLMs perform well above chance on a probing task to detect the presence or absence of specific characters in a token, with larger models generally performing better.
Character-level information is encoded across multiple alphabetic scripts (Latin, Devanagari, Arabic, Cyrillic).
Performance on the character probing task is partially explained by systematic correlations between certain characters and syntactic features (e.g., 's' with plurals, 'y' with adverbs).
Variability in how a word is tokenized across different contexts (due to case, whitespace, or misspellings) provides another mechanism for models to learn character-level information.
Character classification performance is better for rare letters and for characters appearing earlier in tokens, and is not solely driven by high-frequency tokens.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses on static, non-contextualized embeddings rather than contextualized representations from later layers.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to contextualized embeddings from later layers of the model.
Investigate the implications of these findings for improving tokenization schemes, especially in multilingual settings.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) that use subword tokenization schemes can succeed at a variety of language tasks that require characterlevel information, despite lacking explicit access to the character composition of tokens. Here, studying a range of models (e.g., GPT-J, BERT, RoBERTa, GloVe), we probe what word pieces encode about character-level information by training classifiers to predict the presence or absence of a particular alphabetical character in a token, based on its embedding (e.g., probing whether the model embedding for "cat" encodes that it contains the character "a"). We find that these models robustly encode character-level information and, in general, larger models perform better at the task. We show that these results generalize to characters from non-Latin alphabets (Arabic, Devanagari, and Cyrillic). Then, through a series of experiments and analyses, we investigate the mechanisms through which PLMs acquire English-language character information during training and argue that this knowledge is acquired through multiple phenomena, including a systematic relationship between particular characters and particular parts of speech, as well as natural variability in the tokenization of related strings.

papers.title: Improving Multilingual Language Models by Aligning Representations through Steering
papers.research_question: How can multilingual alignment in LLMs be achieved efficiently by targeting a single layer through representation steering, and what does this reveal about internal structures?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method to enhance multilingual LLMs by steering representations at a single layer, achieving performance competitive with translation systems while requiring fewer resources.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation-level steering is an efficient tool for improving multilingual capabilities, providing insights into internal representations and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Single-layer steering significantly improves multilingual performance over baselines like prompt optimization and SFT.
Steering vectors can be shared across structurally similar languages, enabling zero-shot cross-linguistic transfer.
The method approaches the performance of Google Translate, with DPO steering trailing by only 3.08%.
High-resource languages dominate the representation space, and steering helps align low-resource languages.
Steering is most effective in early layers for multilingual models like Aya23, while for models like Llama2, it varies by language resource level.
papers.limitation:
probing by sweeping across all model layers is not scalable for LLMs and is impractical for real-world applications
the learnable steering vector is constrained by its fixed linear direction, limiting its capacity to capture intricate mapping relationships
experiments were focused on single layer and language, lacking multi-objective training
future_direction: Developing context-aware steering mechanisms that adapt dynamically to each prompt
Learning steering vectors by individual tokens rather than fixed vectors
Multi-objective training for simultaneous multi-language and multi-layer steering
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) represent non-English tokens -- a question that remains underexplored despite recent progress. We propose a lightweight intervention method using representation steering, where a learned vector is added to the residual stream at a single model layer to enhance multilingual performance. Through extensive experiments across seven competitive baselines -- including prompt optimization, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), in-context learning, cross-lingual transfer, and translation-based methods-we show that our approach consistently outperforms most alternatives. In particular, it achieves performance on par with production-grade translation systems while requiring far fewer resources. We further explore the complementarity between our method and SFT, demonstrating that steering offers a direct, efficient way to realign internal representations. These findings underscore the potential of activation-level interventions as a powerful tool for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
