Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: How Programming Concepts and Neurons Are Shared in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do code language models represent multiple programming languages and English in their concept space? Specifically, do they use a pivot language, and can we identify language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates how code language models represent programming languages and English, finding that English and certain PLs (like C#) are central in the concept space, and that language-specific neurons exist but are challenging to identify for highly aligned PLs.
papers.conclusion: Our findings deepen our understanding of LLMs’ inner workings in the context of PLs and provide valuable insights for interpretability in code-related tasks.
papers.key_findings:
English and PL keywords appear in intermediate layers with high probabilities in the second half of the layers.
C# is highly aligned with other PLs in the model's concept space.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in bottom layers, while PL-exclusive neurons are in top layers.
For highly aligned PLs (like C# and Java), identifying language-specific neurons is challenging.
The model's concept space is closer to English and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in intermediate layers during translation tasks.
papers.limitation:
The super-parallel dataset is limited to seven languages due to source constraints.
Using keywords to interpret latent embeddings may not be precise because some PL keywords lack direct English meanings or map to multiple tokens.
The analysis is limited to Llama-based architectures; exploring other architectures is needed for broader validation.
papers.abstract: Several studies have explored the mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) in coding tasks, but most have focused on programming languages (PLs) in a monolingual setting. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between multiple PLs and English in the concept space of LLMs. We perform a few-shot translation task on 21 PL pairs using two Llama-based models. By decoding the embeddings of intermediate layers during this task, we observe that the concept space is closer to English (including PL keywords) and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in the second half of the intermediate layers. We analyze neuron activations for 11 PLs and English, finding that while language-specific neurons are primarily concentrated in the bottom layers, those exclusive to each PL tend to appear in the top layers. For PLs that are highly aligned with multiple other PLs, identifying language-specific neurons is not feasible. These PLs also tend to have a larger keyword set than other PLs and are closer to the model's concept space regardless of the input/output PL in the translation task. Our findings provide insights into how LLMs internally represent PLs, revealing structural patterns in the model's concept space. Code is available at https://github.com/cisnlp/code-specific-neurons.

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.research_question: How do the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in Transformers under different learning objectives (machine translation, language modeling, masked language modeling)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes viewing token representation evolution in Transformers through a compression/prediction trade-off, and shows through experiments that different objectives (MT, LM, MLM) lead to distinct patterns of information flow, with MLM exhibiting a two-stage process of context encoding and token reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The learning objective determines the information flow in the model, and the proposed compression/prediction perspective helps explain the behavior and relates findings to prior probing task results, suggesting MLM may be superior for pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
For LM, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past gets lost and predictions about the future get formed.
For MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation; the token identity then gets recreated at the top layer.
For MT, though representations get refined with context, less processing is happening and most information about the word type does not get lost.
Differences due to training objective are much larger than those due to random initialization.
Frequent tokens change more than rare ones in all layers for LM and MT, but for MLM the pattern is different with two stages; rare tokens generally influence more than frequent ones, except in MLM where the model learns not to over-rely on rare tokens before context is understood.
papers.limitation: Direct mutual information estimation from finite samples for densities on multi-dimensional spaces is challenging.
papers.abstract: We seek to understand how the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in deep neural networks under different learning objectives. We focus on the Transformers for our analysis as they have been shown effective on various tasks, including machine translation (MT), standard left-to-right language models (LM) and masked language modeling (MLM). Previous work used black-box probing tasks to show that the representations learned by the Transformer differ significantly depending on the objective. In this work, we use canonical correlation analysis and mutual information estimators to study how information flows across Transformer layers and how this process depends on the choice of learning objective. For example, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past in left-to-right language models gets vanished and predictions about the future get formed. In contrast, for MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation. The token identity then gets recreated at the top MLM layers.

papers.title: RomanLens: The Role Of Latent Romanization In Multilinguality In LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs use Romanization as a bridge in multilingual processing for non-Roman script languages, and do they exhibit latent Romanization in intermediate layers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs implicitly use Romanization as a bridge for non-Roman scripts, exhibiting Latent Romanization in intermediate layers before switching to native scripts. Semantic concepts are encoded similarly across scripts, and Romanized targets emerge earlier in layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implicitly use Romanization as a bridge for non-Roman scripts, exhibiting Latent Romanization in intermediate layers. Romanization facilitates faster progression toward language-specific embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Latent Romanization occurs in intermediate layers during multilingual next-token generation.
LLMs encode semantic concepts similarly regardless of input script (native or Romanized).
When translating into Romanized script, target representations emerge 1-2 layers earlier than in native script.
papers.limitation:
The mechanisms by which LLMs adjust interactions over timesteps during token generation are not fully understood.
Interpretability of non-Roman scripts at latent layers is limited by tokenization schemes.
The selective occurrence and varying intensity of latent romanization across languages is not explained.
future_direction: Applying findings to develop training strategies that enhance performance across diverse linguistic communities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual performance despite being predominantly trained on English-centric corpora. This raises a fundamental question: How do LLMs achieve such multilingual capabilities? Focusing on languages written in non-Roman scripts, we investigate the role of Romanization - the representation of non-Roman scripts using Roman characters - as a potential bridge in multilingual processing. Using mechanistic interpretability techniques, we analyze next-token generation and find that intermediate layers frequently represent target words in Romanized form before transitioning to native script, a phenomenon we term Latent Romanization. Further, through activation patching experiments, we demonstrate that LLMs encode semantic concepts similarly across native and Romanized scripts, suggesting a shared underlying representation. Additionally, for translation into non-Roman script languages, our findings reveal that when the target language is in Romanized form, its representations emerge earlier in the model's layers compared to native script. These insights contribute to a deeper understanding of multilingual representation in LLMs and highlight the implicit role of Romanization in facilitating language transfer.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can inference-time neuron activation steering improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time method that modulates neuron activations to improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by rebalancing shared and language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: CLAS effectively improves cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by steering activations to promote functional divergence, with gains not reliant on geometric alignment to the anchor language.
papers.key_findings:
CLAS achieves average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) on classification and generation benchmarks, respectively.
Performance improvements are driven by functional divergence, with gains correlating with increased language cluster separation rather than closer alignment to English.
CLAS reduces cosine similarity to English for non-anchor languages, indicating a shift away from strict geometric alignment.
Qualitative analysis shows CLAS suppresses repetition loops and verbosity in generation outputs.
The steering parameter alpha can be positive or negative for optimal performance, indicating task- and model-dependent balance between shared and language-specific signals.
papers.limitation:
Analysis and intervention are anchored to English, which may not generalize to other anchor languages.
CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is gender represented in multilingual models? Is the gender concept encoded in shared subspaces across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Gender representation in multilingual models consists of both shared and language-specific components. The most dominant gender directions are shared across languages, enabling good cross-lingual gender classification, but language-specific directions prevent effective cross-lingual gender removal.
papers.conclusion: Gender representation in multilingual models is partially shared across languages, with the most salient directions being shared and less salient ones being language-specific.
papers.key_findings:
Gender classification using linear probes transfers well across languages (English, French, Spanish).
Gender removal using Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) does not transfer well across languages.
Gender subspaces are spanned by a few dominant directions that are shared across languages and other language-specific directions.
The shared gender directions are the most dominant ones (highest predictive power).
The partial sharing explains the discrepancy between transferable classification and non-transferable removal.
papers.limitation:
The study relies on a narrow, binary notion of gender, which does not reflect the full complexity of gender bias.
The analysis is limited to three languages (English, French, Spanish) due to dataset availability.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models were shown to allow for nontrivial transfer across scripts and languages. In this work, we study the structure of the internal representations that enable this transfer. We focus on the representation of gender distinctions as a practical case study, and examine the extent to which the gender concept is encoded in shared subspaces across different languages. Our analysis shows that gender representations consist of several prominent components that are shared across languages, alongside language-specific components. The existence of language-independent and language-specific components provides an explanation for an intriguing empirical observation we make: while gender classification transfers well across languages, interventions for gender removal, trained on a single language, do not transfer easily to others.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Language over Content: Tracing Cultural Understanding in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally represent and process cultural knowledge, and does linguistic form or semantic content dominate their internal path selection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that internal activation paths in multilingual LLMs overlap more for semantically equivalent questions asked in the same language about different cultures than for questions asked in different languages about the same culture, indicating that cultural understanding is strongly mediated by language-specific circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query language affects internal path selection more strongly than target culture, and cultural understanding is mainly stored in language-dependent paths. Politically unique contexts like South and North Korea are reflected in the model's internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Internal path overlap is greater for same-language, cross-country questions than for cross-language, same-country questions, showing a strong language-specific pattern.
The South Korea–North Korea pair exhibits low path overlap and high variability despite linguistic similarity, indicating distinct internal representation patterns.
Multilingual LLMs rely heavily on language-specific circuits when representing and applying cultural knowledge, prioritizing linguistic form over semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on internal path overlap, but interventions or circuit patching could clarify which features drive cultural knowledge processing and how language- and culture-related features interact.
Some country pairs, such as South and North Koreas, show distinct patterns compared to other similar language pairs, yet the reasons remain unclear.
future_direction: Further subdivide cultural knowledge into finer categories and include more languages for a more comprehensive investigation.
Use interventions or circuit patching to clarify which features drive cultural knowledge processing and how language- and culture-related features interact.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used across diverse cultural contexts, making accurate cultural understanding essential. Prior evaluations have mostly focused on output-level performance, obscuring the factors that drive differences in responses, while studies using circuit analysis have covered few languages and rarely focused on culture. In this work, we trace LLMs' internal cultural understanding mechanisms by measuring activation path overlaps when answering semantically equivalent questions under two conditions: varying the target country while fixing the question language, and varying the question language while fixing the country. We also use same-language country pairs to disentangle language from cultural aspects. Results show that internal paths overlap more for same-language, cross-country questions than for cross-language, same-country questions, indicating strong language-specific patterns. Notably, the South Korea-North Korea pair exhibits low overlap and high variability, showing that linguistic similarity does not guarantee aligned internal representation.

papers.title: Are Knowledge and Reference in Multilingual Language Models Cross-Lingually Consistent?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models recall factual knowledge for coreferential statements in a similar manner across languages, how does the mechanism work, and which factors prevent model consistency in multilingual settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual consistency of factual knowledge in multilingual models, identifying bottlenecks related to language characteristics and showing that explicit cross-lingual supervision (code-switching, word alignment) improves consistency more than scaling or instruction tuning.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights limitations in cross-lingual consistency of multilingual models and emphasizes the value of explicit cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for enhancing consistency.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-lingual consistency is lower for languages dissimilar to English in script, family, or geography.
A consistency bottleneck exists in specific middle layers of the models.
Vocabulary expansion offers only slight consistency improvements and relies on deep semantic alignment rather than shared scripts.
Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives significantly improve consistency, while instruction tuning offers limited gains.
Activation patching on feed-forward neurons based on IG2 scores can partially calibrate consistency at test time, showing a causal relationship.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual consistency should be considered to assess cross-lingual transferability, maintain the factuality of the model knowledge across languages, and preserve the parity of language model performance. We are thus interested in analyzing, evaluating, and interpreting cross-lingual consistency for factual knowledge. To facilitate our study, we examine multiple pretrained models and tuned models with code-mixed coreferential statements that convey identical knowledge across languages. Interpretability approaches are leveraged to analyze the behavior of a model in cross-lingual contexts, showing different levels of consistency in multilingual models, subject to language families, linguistic factors, scripts, and a bottleneck in cross-lingual consistency on a particular layer. Code-switching training and cross-lingual word alignment objectives show the most promising results, emphasizing the worthiness of cross-lingual alignment supervision and code-switching strategies for both multilingual performance and cross-lingual consistency enhancement. In addition, experimental results suggest promising result for calibrating consistency in the test time via activation patching.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects: Discrepancy between Performance and Competence
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between performance and competence in LLMs' linguistic understanding? How do LLMs represent form and meaning across languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurolinguistic method (minimal pair probing) to assess LLMs' linguistic competence, revealing a distinction between performance and competence, and showing LLMs have stronger form competence than meaning competence.
papers.conclusion: This study adopts both psycho- and neuro-linguistic approaches to evaluating LLMs, revealing a distinction between linguistic performance and competence, and highlights the limitations of LLMs' semantic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct.
Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence.
Instruction tuning improves performance but does not significantly change competence.
LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning.
LLMs encode form earlier than meaning.
papers.limitation:
Limited range of languages covered in experiments.
Poor German evaluation results potentially due to very long sentences in the DistilLingEval dataset.
Experiments conducted on small-scale LLMs due to computational resource constraints.
COMPS dataset for conceptual understanding is not sufficiently fine-grained, limited to only four types of conceptual relationships.
future_direction: Include experiments covering a wider range of languages.
Construct syntactic minimal pair datasets for German.
Explore larger models to validate and extend generalizability.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the linguistic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding signifier (form) and signified (meaning) by distinguishing two LLM assessment paradigms: psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic. Traditional psycholinguistic evaluations often reflect statistical rules that may not accurately represent LLMs' true linguistic competence. We introduce a neurolinguistic approach, utilizing a novel method that combines minimal pair and diagnostic probing to analyze activation patterns across model layers. This method allows for a detailed examination of how LLMs represent form and meaning, and whether these representations are consistent across languages. We found: (1) Psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic methods reveal that language performance and competence are distinct; (2) Direct probability measurement may not accurately assess linguistic competence; (3) Instruction tuning won't change much competence but improve performance; (4) LLMs exhibit higher competence and performance in form compared to meaning. Additionally, we introduce new conceptual minimal pair datasets for Chinese (COMPS-ZH) and German (COMPS-DE), complementing existing English datasets.

papers.title: What does mBERT layers encode from code-switched data?
papers.research_question: What linguistic information is encoded in different layers of mBERT when processing code-switched data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel mechanism to generate datasets for probing tasks for code-switched data and uses them to analyze mBERT layers, finding that lower layers capture syntactic information better and that the model's performance varies across tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that lower layers of mBERT capture syntactic information better for code-switched data, and that the model cannot perform well on co-reference resolution tasks without fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of mBERT capture syntactic information better for code-switched data.
The model performs better on Tense, Mood, and Number tasks than on Gender and Person tasks.
The last few layers perform poorly compared to lower layers for the probing tasks.
The model cannot perform well on tasks similar to co-reference resolution without fine-tuning.
The trend of lower layers capturing syntactic information is consistent with monolingual studies, even for code-switched data.
papers.limitation:
The generated datasets are heavily imbalanced.
The model cannot perform well on tasks similar to co-reference resolution without fine-tuning.
The study only considers token-level tasks and not sentence-level tasks.
future_direction: Develop a better dataset by addressing the imbalance or discovering new approaches to generate the golden dataset.
Test the performance on other language pairs or triplets.
Work on sentence-level tasks that deal with syntactic structure, such as TopConst.
papers.abstract: Abstract BERT is an encoder transformer model that generates contextual representation in English monolingual data. Multi-lingual BERT (mBERT) extends BERT's capability to more than 104 languages. The better performance in downstream NLP tasks by these models is attributed to the layered architecture. In monolingual data, embedding these layers encodes linguistic information helpful in numerous tasks like Parts of Speech (POS) tagging, Named Entity Recognition (NER), finding structural dependency, etc. We hypothesize that the hidden states contain a lot of valuable information, and investigating the effectiveness of using the pre-trained features extracted from different layers of the mBERT model would help us unravel more linguistic properties of code-switched data. We use probing tasks, which are auxiliary tasks that aid in isolating a linguistic property that helps understand the behavior of each layer within the model. We introduce a novel mechanism using five different probing tasks like gender, mood, number, person, and tense that help highlight and detect linguistic phenomena of interest. We then continue to use these datasets to determine what layers of mBERT are performing better for each task using MCC and F1 measure scores. We observe that the tasks that involved syntactic tasks are better performed at the layers below the 5th layer; as the tasks keep reduced in syntactic importance, the better-performing layers move towards the last layers, reinforcing the behavior seen when the same tests are performed in monolingual corpora.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. Performance % of Attention Heads Kept PS/S STL STL-SP STL-DP MTL-DP STL-SP STL-DP MTL-DP STL STL-DP

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in multilingual LLMs share similarities with English LLMs but with key differences, such as the role of MLPs in extraction and the composition of relation and language in the last token's function vector.
papers.conclusion: These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies—such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition—that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture.
Subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted.
In decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose relation and language in two separate stages.
MLPs play a more prominent role in extraction in multilingual LLMs compared to English LLMs.
papers.limitation: Excluded languages with too few examples, limiting the analysis to a subset of languages.
future_direction: Developing new methodologies for knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying whether models 'think' in English by examining how the function vector is altered across languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: From Tokens to Words: On the Inner Lexicon of LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs encode words internally from sub-word tokens, and if so, how.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally detokenize sub-word tokens into whole-word representations in early to middle layers via an inner lexicon, enabling vocabulary expansion without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The work unravels the word detokenization process in LLMs, showing it occurs in early to middle layers and enables practical applications for optimizing tokenization and inference costs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can distinguish words from nonwords, with the distinction emerging in early to middle layers.
The last token of a word (even if split) can be decoded as the full word, indicating an inner lexicon.
FFN layers are crucial for retrieving full-word representations from the inner lexicon.
Attention patterns show early layers aggregate sub-word tokens, then later layers ignore them as the full word representation forms.
The inner lexicon can be used to expand the model's vocabulary without fine-tuning, reducing token count and maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
22.6% of multi-token words are never successfully decoded, indicating the inner lexicon does not cover all words.
Vocabulary expansion success rate is lower for morphologically rich languages like Arabic (16%).
papers.abstract: Natural language is composed of words, but modern large language models (LLMs) process sub-words as input. A natural question raised by this discrepancy is whether LLMs encode words internally, and if so how. We present evidence that LLMs engage in an intrinsic detokenization process, where sub-word sequences are combined into coherent whole-word representations at their last token. Our experiments show that this process primarily takes place within the early and middle layers of the model. We further demonstrate its robustness to arbitrary splits (e.g., "cats" to "ca" and "ts"), typos, and importantly-to out-of-vocabulary words: when feeding the last token internal representations of such words to the model as input, it can "understand" them as the complete word despite never seeing such representations as input during training. Our findings suggest that LLMs maintain a latent vocabulary beyond the tokenizer's scope. These insights provide a practical, finetuning-free application for expanding the vocabulary of pre-trained models. By enabling the addition of new vocabulary words, we reduce input length and inference iterations, which reduces both space and model latency, with little to no loss in model accuracy.

papers.title: Disentangling Syntax and Semantics in the Brain with Deep Networks
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle syntactic and semantic representations in the brain using deep language models? The paper proposes a taxonomy and method to decompose the shared representations between language models and the brain into distinct linguistic classes (lexical, compositional, syntactic, semantic).
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a versatile framework to isolate distributed representations of linguistic constructs (lexical, compositional, syntactic, semantic) in brain activity using deep language models like GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that linguistic features theorized as discrete symbols can be investigated in artificial and biological neural networks using the proposed framework, revealing distributed representations for syntax and semantics in the brain.
papers.key_findings:
Compositional representations recruit a more widespread cortical network than lexical ones, encompassing bilateral temporal, parietal and prefrontal cortices.
Syntax and semantics are not associated with separated modules but share a common and distributed neural substrate.
The method successfully isolates syntactic representations in GPT-2 by averaging activations from syntactically equivalent sentences.
Brain scores for syntactic and semantic representations are distributed across multiple brain regions, supporting a distributed view of language processing.
The results generalize across layers of GPT-2 and to other transformer architectures, though with lower brain scores.
papers.limitation: The definitions of compositionality and semantics are imperfect; compositionality does not consider properties like systematicity and generalization, and semantics is defined coarsely as the residual after removing syntax.
papers.abstract: The activations of language transformers like GPT-2 have been shown to linearly map onto brain activity during speech comprehension. However, the nature of these activations remains largely unknown and presumably conflate distinct linguistic classes. Here, we propose a taxonomy to factorize the high-dimensional activations of language models into four combinatorial classes: lexical, compositional, syntactic, and semantic representations. We then introduce a statistical method to decompose, through the lens of GPT-2's activations, the brain activity of 345 subjects recorded with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during the listening of ~4.6 hours of narrated text. The results highlight two findings. First, compositional representations recruit a more widespread cortical network than lexical ones, and encompass the bilateral temporal, parietal and prefrontal cortices. Second, contrary to previous claims, syntax and semantics are not associated with separated modules, but, instead, appear to share a common and distributed neural substrate. Overall, this study introduces a versatile framework to isolate, in the brain activity, the distributed representations of linguistic constructs.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: What does Transformer learn about source code?
papers.research_question: What structural information about source code (e.g., syntax tree, data flow, control flow) do transformer-based models learn?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the aggregated attention score and aggregated attention graph to automatically extract structural information from transformer models for source code, and shows that the extracted graphs are meaningful and effective in downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed aggregated attention score and graph provide an effective way to automatically extract structural information from transformers for source code, offering a new perspective for understanding and utilizing model information.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper transformer layers capture more semantic and structural information in source code, as shown by the shift from diagonal to heterogeneous attention patterns.
The aggregated attention graph can automatically extract meaningful program structure (e.g., control flow and data flow edges) from transformer attention heads.
Different attention heads specialize in different semantic relations (e.g., data flow vs. code structure).
Fine-tuning on a specific programming language enhances the model's ability to capture language-specific structural information.
In the Variable Misuse task, graphs automatically extracted from fine-tuned transformers achieve comparable performance to manually designed graphs.
papers.limitation:
The self-attention mechanism is limited in capturing complex relationships such as control flows.
Original pre-trained models are relatively insensitive to language-specific structural information, making further exploration difficult.
future_direction: Explore other semantic information extracted from transformer-based models.
Propose new models to fully utilize task-specific features in different code intelligence tasks.
papers.abstract: In the field of source code processing, the transformer-based representation models have shown great powerfulness and have achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in many tasks. Although the transformer models process the sequential source code, pieces of evidence show that they may capture the structural information (\eg, in the syntax tree, data flow, control flow, \etc) as well. We propose the aggregated attention score, a method to investigate the structural information learned by the transformer. We also put forward the aggregated attention graph, a new way to extract program graphs from the pre-trained models automatically. We measure our methods from multiple perspectives. Furthermore, based on our empirical findings, we use the automatically extracted graphs to replace those ingenious manual designed graphs in the Variable Misuse task. Experimental results show that the semantic graphs we extracted automatically are greatly meaningful and effective, which provide a new perspective for us to understand and use the information contained in the model.

papers.title: Unraveling Babel: Exploring Multilingual Activation Patterns of LLMs and Their Applications
papers.research_question: How do the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs differ when processing different languages, and how can these patterns be leveraged for applications like model pruning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures to study multilingual activation patterns, and uses these patterns to guide language-specific model pruning, reducing computation while maintaining or even improving performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals multilingual activation patterns in LLMs, their connections to language families and instruction tuning, and provides a new effective approach for model pruning and sparse activation.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns differ across languages and correlate with language families and genera.
Multilingual shared experts are concentrated in middle layers, while shallow and deep layers contain more language-specific experts.
Instruction tuning significantly alters activation patterns, with the largest changes in the last layer.
Pruning based on expert activation frequency outperforms random pruning and can exceed the performance of the original unpruned model in some languages.
Different layers exhibit different activation sparsity, so configuring layer-specific pruning rates yields better results.
papers.limitation:
The pruning ratio is limited due to low activation sparsity in most layers of models like Llama 2.
There is a concern that simplified representations may fail to capture the model's out-of-distribution behavior, though evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks provides some mitigation.
future_direction: Extend experiments to a broader array of models and languages.
Explore how to further leverage these insights to utilize and enhance the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous breakthroughs in the field of NLP, but still lack understanding of their internal neuron activities when processing different languages. We designed a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures, and then visually studied the multilingual activation patterns of LLMs through expert activation frequency heatmaps. Through comprehensive experiments on different model families, different model sizes, and different variants, we analyzed the similarities and differences in the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs when processing different languages. Specifically, we investigated the distribution of high-frequency activated experts, multilingual shared experts, whether multilingual activation patterns are related to language families, and the impact of instruction tuning on activation patterns. We further explored leveraging the discovered differences in expert activation frequencies to guide sparse activation and pruning. Experimental results demonstrated that our method significantly outperformed random expert pruning and even exceeded the performance of unpruned models in some languages. Additionally, we found that configuring different pruning rates for different layers based on activation level differences could achieve better results. Our findings reveal the multilingual processing mechanisms within LLMs and utilize these insights to offer new perspectives for applications such as sparse activation and model pruning.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Interactive Visualization and Manipulation of Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and analyze the behavior of neural machine translation, specifically focusing on beam search and attention components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interactive web-based tool for visualizing and manipulating neural machine translation behavior, specifically focusing on beam search and attention mechanisms, to help users understand NMT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interactive tool provides methods to visualize and manipulate NMT, aiding in the understanding of its behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: Switching between internal and external modes: A multiscale learning principle
papers.research_question: How are internal models learned in neural systems? The paper proposes that learning is facilitated by continual switching between internally biased and externally biased modes of processing.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that switching between internally and externally biased modes of processing at multiple timescales generates an error signal that drives learning in neural systems, enabling the construction and refinement of internal models.
papers.conclusion: Switching between internal and external modes is a multiscale learning principle that allows neural circuits to generate error signals for updating internal models, with predictions that disruption of switching impairs learning and integration of new information.
papers.key_findings:
Mode-switching occurs in diverse neural systems (e.g., hippocampus, neocortex) across timescales from milliseconds to hours.
In the hippocampus, alternating phases of theta oscillations separate encoding (external mode) and retrieval (internal mode) and are linked to synaptic plasticity.
In the neocortex, oscillations like alpha rhythms reflect shifts between feedforward (external) and feedback (internal) processing, influencing perception and learning.
Whole-brain states such as awake rest, default mode network activity, and sleep (non-REM/REM cycles) represent large-scale internal/external mode switches that benefit memory consolidation and integration.
