These findings indicate that multilingual LLMs distinguish languages not by surface script features but by latent representational structures shaped by the training corpus. Our analysis provides practical insights for data composition strategies and fairness in multilingual representation learning. All code and analysis scripts are publicly available at: https://github.com/thisiskorea/How-Language-Directions-Align-with-Token-Geometry-in-Multilingual-LLMs.

papers.title: Isolating Culture Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we localize a set of neurons that drives cultural propensities in multilingual LLMs, separate them from language-specific neurons, and modulate them through interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that culture-specific neurons can be identified in multilingual LLMs, are largely separable from language-specific neurons, and can be selectively modulated through interventions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cultural knowledge concentrates in specialized neuron populations predominantly localized in upper layers of multilingual language models and that pure culture neurons play a substantial functional role.
papers.key_findings:
Culture-specific neurons are largely separable from language-specific neurons.
Cultural representations are localized in upper layers of the model.
Different cultures are encoded in distinct neural populations with minimal cross-cultural interference.
Pure culture-specific neurons (not overlapping with language) constitute about 56.7% of culture-related neurons and are functionally important.
Ablation of culture-specific neurons increases perplexity on culturally relevant data, confirming their critical role.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to a small set of open-source models.
Methodology relies on entropy-based metrics and dataset sampling choices.
MUREL covers only six cultures, potentially omitting important cultural phenomena.
Evaluation focuses on neuron ablation and perplexity; future work should include more comprehensive behavioral and downstream assessments.
future_direction: Broadening coverage to additional cultures, languages, and models.
Extending localization to attention heads.
Testing sufficiency via activation scaling and steering, and evaluating intervention effects on downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Language and culture are deeply intertwined, yet it has been unclear how and where multilingual large language models encode culture. Here, we build on an established methodology for identifying language-specific neurons to localize and isolate culture-specific neurons, carefully disentangling their overlap and interaction with language-specific neurons. To facilitate our experiments, we introduce MUREL, a curated dataset of 85.2 million tokens spanning six different cultures. Our localization and intervention experiments show that LLMs encode different cultures in distinct neuron populations, predominantly in upper layers, and that these culture neurons can be modulated largely independently of language-specific neurons or those specific to other cultures. These findings suggest that cultural knowledge and propensities in multilingual language models can be selectively isolated and edited, with implications for fairness, inclusivity, and alignment. Code and data are available at https://github.com/namazifard/Culture_Neurons.

papers.title: Language Surgery in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the naturally emerging representation alignment in LLMs, particularly in the middle layers, and its implications for disentangling language-specific and language-agnostic information. It also explores how this alignment can be utilized for language-specific manipulation without semantic degradation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Inference-Time Language Control (ITLC), a novel method that leverages latent injection at a single middle layer to enable precise cross-lingual language control and mitigate the language confusion problem in LLMs while preserving semantic integrity.
papers.conclusion: This work advances the understanding of representation alignment in LLMs and introduces ITLC as a practical solution for enhancing monolingual and cross-lingual performance by enabling precise language control.
papers.key_findings:
Representation alignment naturally emerges in the middle layers of multilingual LLMs, distinct from the alignment in models with strictly designed objectives like LaBSE.
The aligned representation in LLMs retains more language-specific information compared to strictly aligned models, which is crucial for determining the generation language.
ITLC effectively controls the output language in both monolingual and cross-lingual settings, significantly improving language consistency metrics (LPR).
ITLC mitigates language confusion with minimal semantic loss, as shown by competitive performance compared to PEFT and other test-time intervention methods.
Language vectors extracted from base models are transferable to their instruction-tuned counterparts, indicating robustness of pre-trained language-specific features.
papers.limitation: ITLC exhibits code-switching to English for some languages (e.g., Indonesian, Japanese, Chinese), indicating it may not fully eliminate the source language vector or capture language-specific information well for these languages, potentially requiring language-specific tuning of the scaling factor.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable generalization capabilities across tasks and languages, revolutionizing natural language processing. This paper investigates the naturally emerging representation alignment in LLMs, particularly in the middle layers, and its implications for disentangling language-specific and language-agnostic information. We empirically confirm the existence of this alignment, analyze its behavior in comparison to explicitly designed alignment models, and demonstrate its potential for language-specific manipulation without semantic degradation. Building on these findings, we propose Inference-Time Language Control (ITLC), a novel method that leverages latent injection to enable precise cross-lingual language control and mitigate language confusion in LLMs. Our experiments highlight ITLC's strong cross-lingual control capabilities while preserving semantic integrity in target languages. Furthermore, we demonstrate its effectiveness in alleviating the cross-lingual language confusion problem, which persists even in current large-scale LLMs, leading to inconsistent language generation. This work advances our understanding of representation alignment in LLMs and introduces a practical solution for enhancing their monolingual and cross-lingual performance.

papers.title: How does Alignment Enhance LLMs' Multilingual Capabilities? A Language Neurons Perspective
papers.research_question: How does multilingual alignment enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities from the perspective of language neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a ternary classification of language neurons (specific, related, general) with an identification algorithm, and uses it to analyze how multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' capabilities by promoting shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a ternary neuron classification and shows that multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' multilingual capabilities by promoting shared language-related neurons, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Language-related neurons shared by multiple languages are crucial for multilingual performance, not just language-specific neurons.
Multilingual alignment increases the reliance on shared language-related neurons rather than language-specific neurons.
LLMs' internal multilingual inference process can be divided into four functional stages based on neuron distributions.
Alignment enhances the activation of appropriate neuron types across different stages of inference.
Spontaneous multilingual alignment is facilitated by increased sharing of language-related neurons across languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited experiments on only two models and two datasets due to resource constraints.
No finer-grained analysis of neurons within the same layer.
future_direction: Perform more comprehensive analysis on different models and datasets.
Conduct finer-grained analysis of neurons within layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Alignment is an effective and representative paradigm to enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities, which transfers the capabilities from the high-resource languages to the low-resource languages. Meanwhile, some research on language-specific neurons provides a new perspective to analyze and understand LLMs' mechanisms. However, we find that there are many neurons that are shared by multiple but not all languages and cannot be correctly classified. In this work, we propose a ternary classification methodology that categorizes neurons into three types, including language-specific neurons, language-related neurons, and general neurons. And we propose a corresponding identification algorithm to distinguish these different types of neurons. Furthermore, based on the distributional characteristics of different types of neurons, we divide the LLMs' internal process for multilingual inference into four parts: (1) multilingual understanding, (2) shared semantic space reasoning, (3) multilingual output space transformation, and (4) vocabulary space outputting. Additionally, we systematically analyze the models before and after alignment with a focus on different types of neurons. We also analyze the phenomenon of ''Spontaneous Multilingual Alignment''. Overall, our work conducts a comprehensive investigation based on different types of neurons, providing empirical results and valuable insights to better understand multilingual alignment and multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: An Exploratory Study on Code Attention in BERT
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention mechanism behave on code, and how does it differ from natural language? What code constructs receive the most attention, and can identifier embeddings improve code clone detection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT pays more attention to identifiers and separators in code, and using identifier embeddings instead of [CLS] embeddings improves code clone detection performance.
papers.conclusion: Identifiers are important for code modeling, and using their embeddings improves code clone detection, potentially enabling smaller models with similar performance.
papers.key_findings:
BERT attends more to identifiers and separators in code, unlike in NLP where [CLS] is attended.
Using identifier embeddings improves clone detection by 605% in lower layers and 4% in upper layers for BERT, and 21-24% for CodeBERT.
BERT can predict syntactic entities with high accuracy but fails to predict valid tokens accurately.
papers.limitation:
External threats: dataset choice (CodeSearchNet), task choice (only code clone detection), and language choice (only Java) may limit generalizability.
Conclusion threats: potential bias in sampling code from the dataset.
future_direction: Evaluating the results on other software engineering tasks
Investigating the combination of identifier and separator embeddings
papers.abstract: Many recent models in software engineering introduced deep neural models based on the Transformer architecture or use transformer-based Pre-trained Language Models (PLM) trained on code. Although these models achieve the state of the arts results in many downstream tasks such as code summarization and bug detection, they are based on Transformer and PLM, which are mainly studied in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) field. The current studies rely on the reasoning and practices from NLP for these models in code, despite the differences between natural languages and programming languages. There is also limited literature on explaining how code is modeled. Here, we investigate the attention behavior of PLM on code and compare it with natural language. We pre-trained BERT, a Transformer based PLM, on code and explored what kind of information it learns, both semantic and syntactic. We run several experiments to analyze the attention values of code constructs on each other and what BERT learns in each layer. Our analyses show that BERT pays more attention to syntactic entities, specifically identifiers and separators, in contrast to the most attended token [CLS] in NLP. This observation motivated us to leverage identifiers to represent the code sequence instead of the [CLS] token when used for code clone detection. Our results show that employing embeddings from identifiers increases the performance of BERT by 605% and 4% F1-score in its lower layers and the upper layers, respectively. When identifiers' embeddings are used in CodeBERT, a code-based PLM, the performance is improved by 21-24% in the F1-score of clone detection. The findings can benefit the research community by using code-specific representations instead of applying the common embeddings used in NLP, and open new directions for developing smaller models with similar performance.

papers.title: Hyperpolyglot LLMs: Cross-Lingual Interpretability in Token Embeddings
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models (LLMs) represent relationships between languages in their input token embeddings? Specifically, does the geometry of these embeddings encode language identity or cross-lingual semantic similarity?
papers.core_contribution: The geometry of input token embeddings in multilingual LLMs is interpretable and differs between model families: XLM-RoBERTa embeddings encode language identity (writing systems), while mT5 embeddings encode cross-lingual semantic similarity without explicit parallel training.
papers.conclusion: Input token embeddings of LLMs are interpretable and meaningful, and mT5 accidentally achieves cross-lingual semantic alignment without explicit supervision, a goal that previously required dedicated methods.
papers.key_findings:
XLM-RoBERTa token embeddings linearly separate writing systems with 99.2% accuracy.
mT5 token embeddings have nearest neighbors that are often translations, with an average of 7.61 writing systems in the top 50 neighbors.
The geometry of token embeddings is consistent across parameter scales within the same model family.
mT5 discovers a shared cross-lingual semantic space without explicit parallel data or training objective.
The patterns in token embeddings are interpretable and differ by model family.
papers.limitation: The work is descriptive rather than explanatory; it observes patterns but cannot identify causal factors due to the many differences in model architectures, training methods, and pre-training corpora between LLM families.
future_direction: Explaining factors causing the different token embedding patterns (model architectures, pre-training procedures, data curation).
Exploring the utility of combining low-resource languages with closely related higher-resource languages in pre-training corpora.
Exploring potential applications of cross-lingual representations embedded in LLMs for downstream tasks and model selection.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer learning is an important property of multilingual large language models (LLMs). But how do LLMs represent relationships between languages? Every language model has an input layer that maps tokens to vectors. This ubiquitous layer of language models is often overlooked. We find that similarities between these input embeddings are highly interpretable and that the geometry of these embeddings differs between model families. In one case (XLM-RoBERTa), embeddings encode language: tokens in different writing systems can be linearly separated with an average of 99.2% accuracy. Another family (mT5) represents cross-lingual semantic similarity: the 50 nearest neighbors for any token represent an average of 7.61 writing systems, and are frequently translations. This result is surprising given that there is no explicit parallel cross-lingual training corpora and no explicit incentive for translations in pre-training objectives. Our research opens the door for investigations in 1) The effect of pre-training and model architectures on representations of languages and 2) The applications of cross-lingual representations embedded in language models.

papers.title: On Efficient Transformer-Based Image Pre-training for Low-Level Vision
papers.research_question: How does pre-training act in image processing systems (low-level vision tasks) and what are effective pre-training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes how pre-training affects internal representations in low-level vision tasks and finds that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other strategies.
papers.conclusion: Pre-training plays a central role in developing stronger intermediate representations by incorporating more local information, and its effect is task-specific. Multi-related-task pre-training is highly effective and data-efficient for low-level vision.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution and deraining, yielding significant performance gains, while it hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains.
Multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than single-task or multi-unrelated-task pre-training.
Larger model capacities generally obtain more improvements from pre-training.
Transformers benefit more from pre-training than CNNs, providing higher performance baselines with fewer parameters.
The internal representations of SR and deraining models show clear stages (more local in early layers, more global in higher layers), while denoising models present a relatively uniform structure filled with local information.
papers.limitation:
The study mainly investigates pre-training on synthesized data; future research should explore real-world settings and more tasks, extended to video processing.
The encoder-decoder design uses a fixed downsampling strategy, which may not be optimal for all degradation levels; adaptive downsampling could be better.
future_direction: Explore pre-training in real-world settings and more tasks.
Extend the study to video processing.
Investigate adaptive downsampling based on degradation degrees.
papers.abstract: Pre-training has marked numerous state of the arts in high-level computer vision, while few attempts have ever been made to investigate how pre-training acts in image processing systems. In this paper, we tailor transformer-based pre-training regimes that boost various low-level tasks. To comprehensively diagnose the influence of pre-training, we design a whole set of principled evaluation tools that uncover its effects on internal representations. The observations demonstrate that pre-training plays strikingly different roles in low-level tasks. For example, pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution (SR), yielding significant performance gains, while pre-training hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains. Further, we explore different methods of pre-training, revealing that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other alternatives. Finally, we extend our study to varying data scales and model sizes, as well as comparisons between transformers and CNNs-based architectures. Based on the study, we successfully develop state-of-the-art models for multiple low-level tasks. Code is released at https://github.com/fenglinglwb/EDT.

papers.title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: To what extent does Multilingual BERT learn a cross-lingual representation of syntactic structure? Does mBERT learn universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations; its syntactic subspaces are shared across languages and capture dependency clusters that largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, indicating the model induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations and induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision, which largely agree with the dependency labels of Universal Dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
The structural probe recovers syntactic tree distances in multiple languages from mBERT representations.
The syntactic subspaces are shared across languages, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of syntactic information.
mBERT represents dependency clusters that largely overlap with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, showing it learns universal grammatical relations.
The cross-lingual syntactic subspace is a small part (approx. 32-128 dimensions) of the overall 768-dimensional representation.
Transfer probe performance is substantially correlated with subspace similarity across languages.
papers.limitation:
Cannot tease apart whether transfer performance is caused by subword overlap or by a more fundamental sharing of parameters.
Only conduct a qualitative study in the unsupervised emergence of dependency labels via t-SNE; future work could extend to quantitative results.
Acknowledge issues in interpreting t-SNE plots.
Methods cannot support causal implications for the decisions made by the model.
future_direction: Explore other multilingual models like XLM and XLM-RoBERTa.
Attempt to understand the extent to which the discovered properties have causal implications for the model's decisions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found evidence that Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, is capable of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that some aspects of its representations are shared cross-lingually. To better understand this overlap, we extend recent work on finding syntactic trees in neural networks' internal representations to the multilingual setting. We show that subspaces of mBERT representations recover syntactic tree distances in languages other than English, and that these subspaces are approximately shared across languages. Motivated by these results, we present an unsupervised analysis method that provides evidence mBERT learns representations of syntactic dependency labels, in the form of clusters which largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy. This evidence suggests that even without explicit supervision, multilingual masked language models learn certain linguistic universals.

papers.title: False Friends Are Not Foes: Investigating Vocabulary Overlap in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: Does token overlap facilitate cross-lingual transfer or introduce interference between languages? When and how does the presence of overlapping tokens improve cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: Token overlap in multilingual models promotes cross-lingual semantic alignment and improves transfer performance, with semantically similar overlap being most beneficial.
papers.conclusion: Vocabulary overlap is advantageous for cross-lingual transfer, and tokenizer design should focus on other quality factors rather than reducing overlap.
papers.key_findings:
Models with any vocabulary overlap consistently outperform models with no overlap on XNLI and XQuAD tasks.
Transfer performance generally improves as overlap increases.
Tokens with high semantic similarity across languages contribute most to transfer performance.
Overlap enables embedding spaces to capture cross-lingual semantic relationships, an effect weaker in disjoint vocabularies.
The benefits of overlap vary with typological distance between languages, with high-similarity overlap being more critical for distant pairs.
papers.limitation:
Computational expense limits the number of language pairs studied.
Focus on English-centric language pairs may not generalize to non-English scenarios.
Use of a single tokenizer (XLM-R) may not capture effects of different tokenizer designs.
future_direction: Explore additional language pairs, particularly low-resource languages.
Investigate overlap effects in non-English language pairings.
Examine how overlap interacts with different tokenizers or extended training budgets.
papers.abstract: Subword tokenizers trained on multilingual corpora naturally produce overlapping tokens across languages. Does token overlap facilitate cross-lingual transfer or instead introduce interference between languages? Prior work offers mixed evidence, partly due to varied setups and confounders, such as token frequency or subword segmentation granularity. To address this question, we devise a controlled experiment where we train bilingual autoregressive models on multiple language pairs under systematically varied vocabulary overlap settings. Crucially, we explore a new dimension to understanding how overlap affects transfer: the semantic similarity of tokens shared across languages. We first analyze our models' hidden representations and find that overlap of any kind creates embedding spaces that capture cross-lingual semantic relationships, while this effect is much weaker in models with disjoint vocabularies. On XNLI and XQuAD, we find that models with overlap outperform models with disjoint vocabularies, and that transfer performance generally improves as overlap increases. Overall, our findings highlight the advantages of token overlap in multilingual models and show that substantial shared vocabulary remains a beneficial design choice for multilingual tokenizers.

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: Steering into New Embedding Spaces: Analyzing Cross-Lingual Alignment Induced by Model Interventions in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the finding experts intervention on cross-lingual alignment in multilingual language models?
papers.core_contribution: Intervening on language expert neurons in mLLMs projects embeddings into a new space with enhanced cross-lingual alignment, leading to improved performance on cross-lingual retrieval tasks.
papers.conclusion: The finding-experts intervention enhances cross-lingual alignment in mLLMs, improving retrieval performance, and is recommended for aligning representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The finding experts intervention shifts the embedding space, reducing distances between languages and increasing cross-lingual alignment.
Post-intervention, cross-lingual retrieval accuracy improves by up to 2x in top-1 accuracy.
Within-language similarity is preserved in the new embedding space, as shown by paraphrase retrieval accuracy.
Intervention on random neurons does not yield similar improvements, indicating the importance of targeting expert neurons.
The intervention is most effective when the model has been trained on both the intervention-target and the languages to be aligned.
papers.limitation:
Lack of access to training data and procedures for the models, limiting deeper analysis.
PolyLM-13b behaves as an outlier in the analyses, possibly due to training differences.
Only one intervention method (finding experts) is studied, leaving other approaches for future work.
future_direction: Explore the effect of intervention on alignment in controlled settings with known training data.
Compare different model intervention methods to understand their impact on representation space.
papers.abstract: Aligned representations across languages is a desired property in multilingual large language models (mLLMs), as alignment can improve performance in cross-lingual tasks. Typically alignment requires fine-tuning a model, which is computationally expensive, and sizable language data, which often may not be available. A data-efficient alternative to fine-tuning is model interventions -- a method for manipulating model activations to steer generation into the desired direction. We analyze the effect of a popular intervention (finding experts) on the alignment of cross-lingual representations in mLLMs. We identify the neurons to manipulate for a given language and introspect the embedding space of mLLMs pre- and post-manipulation. We show that modifying the mLLM's activations changes its embedding space such that cross-lingual alignment is enhanced. Further, we show that the changes to the embedding space translate into improved downstream performance on retrieval tasks, with up to 2x improvements in top-1 accuracy on cross-lingual retrieval.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Reinforcement Learning Using Attention Augmented Agents
papers.research_question: How can an attention mechanism be used to create interpretable reinforcement learning agents while maintaining competitive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a soft attention model for RL that provides interpretability through attention maps while achieving competitive performance on ATARI games.
papers.conclusion: The attention mechanism provides interpretability and competitive performance, and the agent learns meaningful attention strategies for decision making.
papers.key_findings:
The agent learns to attend to task-relevant objects like the player, enemies, and score.
The agent can react appropriately to novel, unseen configurations of the environment.
The agent performs forward planning/scanning by attending to possible future trajectories.
The agent uses 'trip wires' (attention at strategic points) to trigger specific actions.
The agent's queries separate 'what' (content) and 'where' (spatial) information.
papers.abstract: Inspired by recent work in attention models for image captioning and question answering, we present a soft attention model for the reinforcement learning domain. This model uses a soft, top-down attention mechanism to create a bottleneck in the agent, forcing it to focus on task-relevant information by sequentially querying its view of the environment. The output of the attention mechanism allows direct observation of the information used by the agent to select its actions, enabling easier interpretation of this model than of traditional models. We analyze different strategies that the agents learn and show that a handful of strategies arise repeatedly across different games. We also show that the model learns to query separately about space and content (`where' vs. `what'). We demonstrate that an agent using this mechanism can achieve performance competitive with state-of-the-art models on ATARI tasks while still being interpretable.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is Reflected in Brain Responses
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? Does the low-dimensional structure of these representations correspond to brain responses during language processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a low-dimensional structure in the space of language representations and shows that this structure can predict how well each representation maps to human brain responses to natural language, suggesting it captures part of the brain's natural language representation hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure in language representations reflects the brain's natural language processing hierarchy, suggesting that the embedding captures some part of the brain's representation structure.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional structure exists in the space of language representations, with the first MDS dimension capturing a progression from word embeddings to syntactic/semantic tasks to next-word embeddings.
The representation embeddings can predict fMRI encoding model performance, indicating a link between the representation space and brain responses.
Projecting the first MDS dimension onto the brain recovers known language processing hierarchies, with early auditory cortex explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later layers.
Most pairs of representations can be correctly matched to their brain response patterns using the representation embeddings.
The low-dimensional structure is consistent across different language models and translation models.
papers.limitation: Negative discriminability scores for some representation pairs, possibly due to disconnect between task affinities and brain representations, e.g., for GloVe next-word embedding.
papers.abstract: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks. This method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation: Mutual Opportunities and Open Challenges
papers.research_question: Can LLMs leverage both their robust capabilities (in English) and their multilingual knowledge (in non-English languages) during inference to further unlock their multilingual potential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation (X Transplant), a probing framework that transplants latent activations across languages at inference time to unlock multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs, revealing underutilized potential.
papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: LinguaMap: Which Layers of LLMs Speak Your Language and How to Tune Them?
papers.research_question: Where in the model do language-specific behaviors–such as language consistency, dominance bias, and multilingual interference–reside, and can they be isolated to enable efficient and effective multilingual adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to evaluate language control in multilingual LLMs, reveals a three-phase internal structure (semantic alignment, reasoning, language generation), and proposes selective fine-tuning of the final layers to improve language consistency without sacrificing task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that layer-localization of language control enables efficient multilingual adaptation via selective fine-tuning, achieving high language consistency with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit two key failure modes: the multilingual transfer bottleneck (correct language, incorrect task response) and the language consistency bottleneck (correct task response, wrong language).
Internal analysis using logit lens and hidden state similarity reveals a three-phase structure: early layers align inputs into a shared semantic space, middle layers perform task reasoning, and late layers drive language-specific generation.
Selective fine-tuning of only the final layers responsible for language control achieves over 98% language consistency across six languages while fine-tuning only 3–5% of parameters, matching the performance of full-scope fine-tuning.
The method is effective on models like Qwen-3-32B and Bloom-7.1B, improving language consistency from <20% to 98+% without compromising task accuracy.
Code-switched prompting severely degrades language consistency, highlighting a disconnect between task competence and language control in multilingual LLMs.
papers.abstract: Despite multilingual pretraining, large language models often struggle with non-English tasks, particularly in language control, the ability to respond in the intended language. We identify and characterize two key failure modes: the multilingual transfer bottleneck (correct language, incorrect task response) and the language consistency bottleneck (correct task response, wrong language). To systematically surface these issues, we design a four-scenario evaluation protocol spanning MMLU, MGSM, and XQuAD benchmarks. To probe these issues with interpretability, we extend logit lens analysis to track language probabilities layer by layer and compute cross-lingual semantic similarity of hidden states. The results reveal a three-phase internal structure: early layers align inputs into a shared semantic space, middle layers perform task reasoning, and late layers drive language-specific generation. Guided by these insights, we introduce selective fine-tuning of only the final layers responsible for language control. On Qwen-3-32B and Bloom-7.1B, this method achieves over 98 percent language consistency across six languages while fine-tuning only 3-5 percent of parameters, without sacrificing task accuracy. Importantly, this result is nearly identical to that of full-scope fine-tuning (for example, above 98 percent language consistency for both methods across all prompt scenarios) but uses a fraction of the computational resources. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to leverage layer-localization of language control for efficient multilingual adaptation.

papers.title: Neural FOXP2 -- Language Specific Neuron Steering for Targeted Language Improvement in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can a chosen language (Hindi or Spanish) be made the default language in an LLM by mechanistically steering language-specific neurons, without full retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Neural FOXP2 is a three-stage method that identifies a sparse set of language-selective neurons via sparse autoencoders and steers them using low-rank directions, making a target language the model's default without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Neural FOXP2 demonstrates that targeted language improvement can be achieved through mechanistic, inference-time steering of a sparse set of language neurons, providing a surgical alternative to retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Neural FOXP2 improves Hindi and Spanish performance across machine translation, question answering, natural language inference, and summarization tasks.
The method shifts the model's language prior, making the target language the default generation channel under weak prompting.
Language defaultness is governed by a sparse, low-rank control circuit that can be isolated and steered.
The intervention is surgical, editing only a small set of SAE features in a specific layer window, preserving task semantics and minimizing cross-lingual regression.
The method provides a mechanistic control knob for language preference, avoiding the need for full retraining or fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The method requires specific hooks at the intervention layers and recomputation of artifacts if the model checkpoint, tokenizer, or hook specification changes.
Metric gains (e.g., early token mass) do not always translate to a natural start in the target language, with failure modes including transliteration wins, named-entity dominance, and format-token bias.
papers.abstract: LLMs are multilingual by training, yet their lingua franca is often English, reflecting English language dominance in pretraining. Other languages remain in parametric memory but are systematically suppressed. We argue that language defaultness is governed by a sparse, low-rank control circuit, language neurons, that can be mechanistically isolated and safely steered. We introduce Neural FOXP2, that makes a chosen language (Hindi or Spanish) primary in a model by steering language-specific neurons. Neural FOXP2 proceeds in three stages: (i) Localize: We train per-layer SAEs so each activation decomposes into a small set of active feature components. For every feature, we quantify English vs. Hindi/Spanish selectivity overall logit-mass lift toward the target-language token set. Tracing the top-ranked features back to their strongest contributing units yields a compact language-neuron set. (ii) Steering directions: We localize controllable language-shift geometry via a spectral low-rank analysis. For each layer, we build English to target activation-difference matrices and perform layerwise SVD to extract the dominant singular directions governing language change. The eigengap and effective-rank spectra identify a compact steering subspace and an empirically chosen intervention window (where these directions are strongest and most stable). (iii) Steer: We apply a signed, sparse activation shift targeted to the language neurons. Concretely, within low to mid layers we add a positive steering along the target-language dominant directions and a compensating negative shift toward the null space for the English neurons, yielding controllable target-language defaultness.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: What language-specific features exist in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, and how can they be identified and analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-LAPE, a method to identify language-specific features in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, showing these features are interpretable, influence model behavior, and can be used for language identification.
papers.conclusion: SAE-LAPE can identify interpretable, language-specific features in multilingual LLMs that causally influence model behavior and can be applied to tasks like language identification.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific features exist and are interpretable, primarily located in middle to final layers of the model.
Suppressing language-specific features increases perplexity in the corresponding language, while activating them can shift the model's output towards that language.
Language-specific features can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText, while offering more interpretability.
Features show a hierarchical processing of linguistic information, from morphemes in early layers to complex sentence structures and discourse patterns in deeper layers.
Some features capture stylistic patterns (e.g., conversational vs. formal) and language-specific cultural or geopolitical concepts.
papers.limitation: Interpretations of features may be biased toward the top activating examples, which could come from languages other than the primary one the feature is associated with.
papers.abstract: Understanding the multilingual mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) provides insight into how they process different languages, yet this remains challenging. Existing studies often focus on individual neurons, but their polysemantic nature makes it difficult to isolate language-specific units from cross-lingual representations. To address this, we explore sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for their ability to learn monosemantic features that represent concrete and abstract concepts across languages in LLMs. While some of these features are language-independent, the presence of language-specific features remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce SAE-LAPE, a method based on feature activation probability, to identify language-specific features within the feed-forward network. We find that many such features predominantly appear in the middle to final layers of the model and are interpretable. These features influence the model's multilingual performance and language output and can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText along with more interpretability. Our code and complete figures are available at https://github.com/LyzanderAndrylie/language-specific-features

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: Understanding Early Word Learning in Situated Artificial Agents
papers.research_question: How do neural network-based agents learn to ground words in a simulated 3D world, and do they exhibit human-like word learning biases and dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel layerwise attention method for visualizing semantic representations in a grounded language learning agent, and shows that the agent exhibits human-like word learning dynamics and biases that depend on training distribution.
papers.conclusion: The agent can learn word meanings from raw pixel input and actions, and analysis of its representations reveals similarities to human word learning, suggesting such agents could be used as models for studying language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
The agent exhibits a vocabulary spurt similar to human infants, with word learning accelerating after an initial slow period.
Curriculum learning and an auxiliary reward prediction loss speed up word learning.
The agent develops a shape or color bias depending on the distribution of word types during training, supporting the idea that such biases emerge from environmental statistics.
Layerwise attention reveals that color and shade words activate lower-level visual features, while shape words activate higher-level features, and direction words rely more on action grounding.
Word embeddings cluster according to semantic and syntactic categories.
papers.limitation:
The agent receives symbolic lexical stimuli and does not need to segment the speech stream.
The agent does not learn a new label after a single experience (fast-mapping).
The environment lacks social cues and pragmatic inference due to a single agent.
The visual complexity does not match the real world.
future_direction: Develop end-to-end models that can jointly apply multiple different mechanisms with richer input streams to handle more phenomena observed in infant word learning.
papers.abstract: Neural network-based systems can now learn to locate the referents of words and phrases in images, answer questions about visual scenes, and execute symbolic instructions as first-person actors in partially-observable worlds. To achieve this so-called grounded language learning, models must overcome challenges that infants face when learning their first words. While it is notable that models with no meaningful prior knowledge overcome these obstacles, researchers currently lack a clear understanding of how they do so, a problem that we attempt to address in this paper. For maximum control and generality, we focus on a simple neural network-based language learning agent, trained via policy-gradient methods, which can interpret single-word instructions in a simulated 3D world. Whilst the goal is not to explicitly model infant word learning, we take inspiration from experimental paradigms in developmental psychology and apply some of these to the artificial agent, exploring the conditions under which established human biases and learning effects emerge. We further propose a novel method for visualising semantic representations in the agent.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: Is a cute puyfred cute? Context-dependent form-meaning systematicity in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs represent the valence of pseudowords in isolation and in context, and how does context affect these representations?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs capture systematic form-valence mappings in pseudowords, and pseudowords affect sentence representations similarly to words, but models differ in how they contextualize pseudowords.
papers.conclusion: LLMs capture form-valence systematicity and show different contextualization patterns for pseudowords, providing insights into the form-meaning interface in language learning and processing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs capture pseudoword valence in static embeddings, with correlations to human ratings.
In context, some LLMs (M-BERT, GPT-2, LLaMa 3.2) rely heavily on sentence valence to represent pseudowords, while RoBERTa is more sensitive to pseudoword valence.
Pseudowords influence sentence representations, and the effect is similar to that of words.
The influence of pseudowords on sentence valence is small but systematic.
Two cognitive profiles emerge: context-dominant and form-sensitive.
papers.limitation:
Only considers English pseudowords and sentences.
Valence is only one semantic dimension, not encompassing meaning.
Lack of human behavioral data for comparison.
Only written pseudowords, not spoken or signed.
Assumes a full-fledged vocabulary, not developmentally plausible.
future_direction: Investigate differences between overlapping n-grams and non-overlapping tokens in capturing form-meaning relations.
Collect human behavioral data for pseudowords in context across languages.
Extend to other semantic dimensions beyond valence.
papers.abstract: We investigate static and contextualized embeddings for English pseudowords across a variety of Large Language Models (LLMs), to study (i) how these models represent semantic attributes of strings they encounter for the very first time and how (ii) these representations interact with sentence context.We zoom in on a key semantic attribute, valence, which plays an important role in theories of language processing, acquisition, and evolution.Across three experiments, we show that pseudoword valence is encoded in meaningful ways both in isolation and in context, and that, in some LLMs, pseudowords affect the representation of whole sentences similarly to words.This highlights how, at least for most LLMs we surveyed, pseudowords and words are not qualitatively different constructs.Our study confirms that LLMs capture systematic mappings between form and valence, and shows how different LLMs handle the contextualisation of pseudowords differently.Our findings provide a first computational exploration of how sub-lexical distributional patterns influence the valence of novel strings in context, offering useful insights for theories on the formmeaning interface and how it affects language learning and processing.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Models of Source Codes
papers.research_question: To what extent do pretrained models of source code capture information about syntactic and semantic properties of code, and how are these properties affected by code-specific pretraining objectives, model size, encoder vs. decoder representations, and finetuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a set of diagnostic probing tasks for source code and uses them to show that pretrained models capture syntactic and some semantic information but lack deeper semantic understanding, and that code-specific pretraining objectives help while finetuning can degrade certain code properties.
papers.conclusion: The proposed probing toolkit reveals that pretrained models of code capture basic code properties but lack deeper semantic understanding, and that code-specific pretraining objectives and careful finetuning are important for maintaining code understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained models of code contain information about syntactic structure, namespaces, data flow, and naming, but show limited understanding of deeper semantics like semantic equivalence.
Models pretrained with code-specific objectives (e.g., CodeT5, GraphCodeBERT) perform better on tasks related to those objectives.
Encoder representations are generally more informative for probing than decoder representations.
Model size has a limited effect on probing performance in most tasks.
Finetuning, especially on discriminative downstream tasks, can lead to loss of syntactic and semantic information captured during pretraining.
papers.limitation:
The probing tasks do not cover all possible aspects of source code.
Experiments are limited to Java and Python, and it would be interesting to compare on low-level languages like C/C++.
Linear probes may be limited in capacity, though similar results were found with an MLP.
Only open-sourced pretrained checkpoints are considered.
future_direction: Extend probing to low-level languages like C/C++.
Compare performance across a wider range of model sizes.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models are widely used for solving challenging code processing tasks, such as code generation or code summarization. Traditionally, a specific model architecture was carefully built to solve a particular code processing task. However, recently general pretrained models such as CodeBERT or CodeT5 have been shown to outperform task-specific models in many applications. While pretrained models are known to learn complex patterns from data, they may fail to understand some properties of source code. To test diverse aspects of code understanding, we introduce a set of diagnostic probing tasks. We show that pretrained models of code indeed contain information about code syntactic structure, the notions of identifiers, and namespaces, but they may fail to recognize more complex code properties such as semantic equivalence. We also investigate how probing results are affected by using code-specific pretraining objectives, varying the model size, or finetuning.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens.
